evidence_quotes.quote: The component has the dual objectives of developing sustainable water supply and sanitation systems in low income urban communities and of facilitating a process of participatory institution building at the community level
The emphasis is on relational networks and broad band communication between levels rather than institution building as such at either the community or municipal level.

It is used here as a tool to open up the framework within which urban poverty is discussed, a Foucauldian attempt to free that which purports to be natural in order to alter both the theoretical parameters and the empirical interventions.
The project description is drawn from an outline in the Zambia Urban Poverty Assessment (World Bank 1994: 49,50).
It is expected that financial investment will take place up to a year after project start up to allow for the facilitation of participatory structures

criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban water supply and sanitation infrastructure and service provision for low-income urban communities (compounds) in Lusaka and the Copperbelt cities of Zambia.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, this paper would satisfy Criterion 2 itself because it discusses institutional and governance dimensions of urban water and sanitation delivery (community participation structures, municipal council bureaucratic reorientation, NGO partnerships, and donor capital financing), though plain_criterion2_decision remains exclude because the paper fails Criterion 3 (E05, non-empirical essay/project overview). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is no: the paper critiques macro-development poverty discourse ('Fordist' vs. flexible investment) and describes participatory project delivery and community facilitation in a World Bank project rather than empirically examining a legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access (mentioning organizational preconditions and a per-capita project investment ceiling/upfront O&M contribution only as descriptive features of prospective project design).
criterion_notes.c3: No empirical study design, data collection methodology, sample, or primary empirical evidence is reported ( nor is it a systematic empirical synthesis). The article is a Foucauldian theoretical/conceptual essay on urban poverty and infrastructure discourse paired with a brief policy description of a World Bank project in its initial stages of implementation drawn from a secondary World Bank (1994) outline -> exclude as E05.
criterion_notes.c4: No empirical service-access outcome of an evaluated exposure is measured or reported. The Zambian project component described was only in the initial stages of implementation (with financial investment expected up to a year after start-up), and access problems in Lusaka are cited only as secondary background illustrations (e.g., World Bank 1994; Rakodi 1987).
criterion_notes.c5: Lacks an identifiable empirical study design, sample, and evaluated exposure-outcome relationship because it is a conceptual essay and prospective project overview.

study_design: Theoretical/conceptual essay and prospective project policy overview (non-empirical)
population_and_sample: Low-income urban communities in Lusaka and the Copperbelt cities, Zambia (no empirical sample reported)
exposure: Flexible, participatory urban water and sanitation project delivery and development discourse (low-income component of the World Bank Zambia Urban Restructuring and Water Supply Project)
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Cottam (1997) is a Foucauldian theoretical and policy essay in IDS Bulletin critiquing orthodox urban poverty and 'Fordist' infrastructure discourse, illustrated with a brief prospective overview of the low-income component of the World Bank-funded Zambia Urban Restructuring and Water Supply Project. As Footnote 3 notes, the project description is drawn from an outline in World Bank (1994), the project was only in the initial stages of implementation (with financial investment expected up to a year after start-up), and the article reports no empirical methods, primary data, sample, or measured access outcomes. In addition, under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, the paper focuses on macro-development discourse and participatory project delivery rather than examining a rule-type legal/administrative mechanism governing service access; even under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded for lack of empirical evidence (E05).
